events.text: River bandits come at the landing of {pw_kingdom}, and you beat them. What they leave behind, their strength and their nerve, rises off them like steam, and the hunger drinks it. A lean ferry-warden with a lantern pole watches from the boat. {npc}. "I saw a town after a glutton passed once," {he} says. "Full granaries, and nobody in them hungry for anything. Then the sky went dark."
events.arc: The Glutton of the River Towns

effects.log: {npc} holds the lantern up to your face for a long moment. "Honest, at least," {he} says, and lets you ride the ferry for free.

choices.text: Say the bandits were simply tired

effects.log: {npc} spits into the river. "Tired men do not walk off lighter than they came." {He} writes your name in the ferry-book, under a line you cannot read.

choices.text: Ask what the dark sky was

effects.log: "The god of {b10_world} looking down," says {npc}. "Folk say the god made the river and watches who drinks too much of it." For no reason at all, you remember the cold of a river being poured.

events.text: {npc}, the ferry-warden of the river towns, turns the pages of an old ferry-book and stops. "A glutton crossed here, long before my grandmother," {he} says. "It says the hunger went quiet at the end, and the sky looked away, and the towns ate well for a hundred years." {He} looks at you. "It says the glutton had your way of standing."
events.arc: The Glutton of the River Towns

effects.log: "Then the book was right to keep a page for you," says {npc}, and for the first time the ferry-warden smiles.

choices.text: Say nothing, and listen to the hunger

effects.log: The hunger says one word, very quietly: "Again." It is not hungry when it says it. Overhead the clouds part, and close, as if someone had decided not to look.

events.text: Market day in a river town of {pw_kingdom}: smoked fish, new bread, a whole square of plenty, and the hunger smells all of it. That noon a cloud stands over the square in the shape of an eye. People point. {npc} pushes through to you. "Every glutton gets the eye," {he} says. "Feast, and it opens wider. Fast, and it may close."
events.arc: The Glutton of the River Towns

effects.log: You walk out of the square with your hands in your sleeves and keep walking until dusk. The eye thins to a wisp. {npc} follows at a distance, and says nothing, which from {him} is praise.

choices.text: Feast, and stare back at the sky

effects.log: You eat the square. The hunger roars, warm and full, and the eye over the town opens wide enough to see the blue behind it. {npc} turns away.

events.text: A river-ox gone wild tramples the nets of three families. You bring it down in the shallows, and what it leaves, a great slow warmth, starts to rise. Before the hunger can move, {npc} is there with a net-hook. "That is the town's meat for a winter," {he} says. "Not yours."
events.arc: The Glutton of the River Towns

effects.log: You hold the hunger back with both hands. {npc} drags the ox ashore, and the families share it out on the landing. The ferry child Pip brings you the first bowl.
You are faster. The warmth pours into you, and the ox is only an ox afterwards, heavy and ordinary. {npc} looks at it, and then at you, for a long time.

events.text: Fasting has a price. You grow thin by the river, and the hunger gnaws at night like a dog at a door. {npc} comes up the landing with a parcel from {his} own stores: smoked eel, two loaves, a jar of river honey. "It is not much," {he} says. "It is what the warden can spare."
events.arc: The Glutton of the River Towns

effects.log: You eat it a bite at a time. It tastes of rain and nets and patience. For the first time in this life, the hunger says thank you.

choices.text: Give it to the ferry child

effects.log: Pip eats the honey with both hands. {npc} watches, and then sits down beside you on the cold step without a word.

events.text: The second sign: at the landing the river runs backwards for an hour, and the towns whisper that their god is angry with someone. {npc} comes with a writ of the League of Kingdoms' Wardens, the road-keepers' seal on it. "Leave the river towns," {he} says, "or I pole you off the landing myself."
events.arc: The Glutton of the River Towns

ok.log: You win. {npc} goes into the shallows, lantern and all, and comes up spluttering. The hunger drinks what rises off {his} pride before you can stop it.

fail.log: The pole is quicker than it looks. You wake on the far bank with river weed in your hair and a lump on your head.

choices.text: Give back what you took: feed a town from your purse

effects.log: You buy a whole market's bread and give it away on the landing. {npc} folds the writ and puts it in {his} coat. "Once," {he} says. Over the river the sky turns its face aside.

events.text: By the ferry stands a small temple to the god of {b10_world}, its roof patched with river reed. Old Hanne, its priestess, is praying aloud that the god will look away from the glutton in the towns. Hanne does not know it is you. Neither, quite, does the god, which was also you. {npc} kneels in the back row, and {his} jaw is tight.
events.arc: The Glutton of the River Towns

choices.text: Kneel beside Hanne and pray honestly

effects.log: You pray to yourself to look away from yourself. It is the strangest prayer of your life, and it is heard. The clouds over the temple thin.

choices.text: Leave an offering and go quietly

effects.log: You leave a coin and a loaf on the altar. Hanne blesses you without looking up. The blessing is yours, and it fits like an old coat.

choices.text: Ask Hanne what the god was like

effects.log: "They say the god laughed when the first river ran," says Hanne, "and wept when the first town burned." You find you remember both.

events.text: Two signs given, and the hunger understands something. "The eye," it says, slow and thick. "I know the eye. It made the river I drink from." It wants to grow quiet, so quiet that the sky can close and stop looking. {npc} stands beside you on the landing, the ferry-book shut. "If it goes quiet," {he} says, "the towns will never know it was here."
events.arc: The Glutton of the River Towns

effects.log: The hunger lies down in you like a dog by a fire, and for the first time it is full without eating anything. Overhead the sky closes its eye.
"Not yet," you tell it. It grumbles, and grows anyway, into something that knows how to wait at a ferry.

events.text: Two signs, and the towns lock their doors at dusk. You stand on the landing and look up, and the eye in the cloud looks down, and you remember, all at once, being the eye: making the river, watching who drank. {npc} holds the lantern between you and the sky. "Well?" {he} says. "Which of you blinks?"
events.arc: The Glutton of the River Towns

effects.log: You lift a hand the way you once lifted it over the whole world, and the eye in the cloud closes. The hunger falls quiet, startled into manners.
You stare until the sky gives way. The hunger quiets because it has won, which is not the same as being tamed.

events.text: Dusk at the landing. {npc} trims the lantern and does not look at you. "There is one more thing the hunger can do," {he} says. "It can go into the river, and the river can carry it out past every town on its banks. They would eat well forever, and never know why." {He} sets the lantern down. "Not today. But I wanted you to know there was a door."
events.arc: The Glutton of the River Towns

effects.log: "Do not thank me," says {npc}. "Thank the river." But {he} sits with you until the ferry comes.

choices.text: Say you will think about it on the ferry

effects.log: You ride the ferry across and back, three times. The river is very patient with you.

events.text: {npc} finds you on the landing in the dark. "If you ever walk into the river with that hunger," {he} says roughly, "I will keep a lamp lit here. That is all. I wanted you to know." {He} does not say it is a kindness. It is the only kindness the ferry-warden has ever spoken aloud.
events.arc: The Glutton of the River Towns

effects.log: {npc} grunts. The lamp, when you look back from the road, is already lit.

choices.text: Tell {him} to keep the lamp for the living

effects.log: "Who do you think I meant?" says {npc}. It takes you most of the road home to understand.

events.text: Ding! The System finds a milestone on the high road of {pw_kingdom}: an old stone, rubbed smooth by hands. [SIGN IN?] As you touch it a traveller with a road-lute sings the next line of a song you did not know you knew. {npc}, a road-singer. "Every stone on this road has a verse," {he} says. "Funny. That one never had one until you touched it."

choices.text: Ask {him} to teach you the verses

effects.log: {npc} sings you seven milestones before sundown. The System marks each one with a quiet ding, as if it were keeping time.
"The god of {b10_world}," says {npc}. "Walked the roads before there were any, and left a stone wherever it rested." You look at your own feet for a while.

choices.text: Sign in, and walk on alone

effects.log: The stone hums under your hand. Behind you {npc} sings your verse once more, to no one, and keeps it.

events.text: {npc}, a road-singer, stops strumming when you touch the milestone. "There is a verse for a traveller who signed every road of this world once," {he} says. "It is the last verse of the long song. Nobody sings it, because nobody knows who it is about." {He} plays the first line, and the stone under your hand grows warm.

effects.log: You sing it without knowing how. {npc} lowers the lute and stares at you. "Well," {he} says. "Now somebody knows."

choices.text: Keep your hand on the stone

effects.log: The System counts something under its breath. Ding. The stone gives more than any stone has given before.

events.text: The road splits at a crossing. East runs a kingdom you blessed long ago as its god: green fields, fat milestones, double pay. West runs a kingdom you once cursed in a temper, and its stones are cracked and hungry. "Every traveller takes the east road," says {npc}. "The west stones have not been signed in a hundred years. They charge, you know. For what their god did."

choices.text: Take the west road and pay its debt

effects.log: The first cracked stone takes your coin and gives you almost nothing back. The second sighs. {npc} sings a verse for it that nobody has sung in a century.
The blessed stones pay twice, warm as bread. You grow rich in points and the System sings. {npc} looks back at the west road once, and follows you.

events.text: In a village on the old temple road a boy is chipping a milestone to sell as luck-stone. The village is poor; the stone is the only thing it has. {npc} watches you. "You can sign in on what is left of it," {he} says, "or you can sign in somewhere else, and leave them their luck."

choices.text: Pay the boy for the stone, and leave it standing

effects.log: The boy looks at the coins and then at the stone, and puts the chisel away. The village sings that night. You can hear {npc} leading it.

choices.text: Sign in on what is left

effects.log: The stone gives a thin ding, and the boy goes on chipping. It is not your business, the System says. It sounds almost sure.

events.text: The cursed roads are long and the debts are heavy. Your purse is thin and your boots are thinner, and the points come slowly. But in the west the people have started to leave bread at the milestones you signed. {npc} sings for them at every inn. "They think the god has come back," {he} says. "I have not told them which one."

choices.text: Tell them it was only a traveller

effects.log: They do not believe you. They leave you bread anyway. It is the best bread you have ever eaten.

choices.text: Sing with {him} at the next inn

effects.log: You sing badly and the inn sings back. A cracked stone outside the window, for the first time in a hundred years, rings.

events.text: Only the blessed roads, and the points pile up. But the stones of the east have started to know you, and one evening a whole line of them goes quiet when you pass, the way a dog goes quiet when it sees someone it does not trust. {npc} tunes the lute. "They are fond of their god," {he} says, "not of greed."

choices.text: Turn back and sign a cursed stone

effects.log: You walk a day west and pay a cracked stone what it asks. The east road hums again when you return. {npc} stops frowning.
You walk on. The stones pay, a little less each year, and you tell yourself that is only the road.

events.text: On the river road a League of Kingdoms' Warden stops you: a stout woman named Ottil with a ledger of every traveller. "You touch every milestone," Ottil says. "Folk notice. Some say you are a thief of luck. Some say you are a pilgrim." {npc} plays a chord behind you, helpfully.

ok.log: You tell Ottil the truth, more or less: you are only saying hello to old stones. Ottil laughs and stamps your pass. "Mind you say goodbye too."

fail.log: Ottil is not charmed. The Warden makes you walk the river road twice under the Warden's eye, and fines you for the trouble.

effects.log: You sign in at the next stone in front of Ottil. It rings. Ottil writes for a long time, and lets you go with a look you cannot read.

events.text: Four places of {b10_world} signed, and at the last one the System goes still. Ding. [THE ROADS REMEMBER WHO LAID THEM.] Every milestone you have ever touched hums at once, from the high roads to the river. {npc} drops the lute. "They are singing," {he} says. "All of them. The long song. They know the last verse now."

choices.text: Sing the last verse with them

effects.log: You sing it, and the roads sing back, and for one evening every traveller in {b10_world} hears it at once.
You listen to the roads you made singing about the one who made them. It is like hearing your own name in a crowd.

events.text: At a crossing no map shows, four signed roads meet, and the stone at the centre is the oldest you have touched. Ding. The System reads it and stops. [THIS STONE WAS SET BY YOUR HAND.] Moss and all. {npc} sits on the verge and plays very softly, so as not to interrupt.

choices.text: Sign in, and stay a while

effects.log: You sit with your back to the stone you set before there were roads. The System does not count anything for a long time.

choices.text: Ask {him} for a verse for it

effects.log: {npc} makes one up on the spot. It is a bad verse, and the stone loves it.

events.text: {npc} walks you to the edge of the signed roads, playing all the while. "There is a verse after the last one," {he} says. "About a traveller who became a milestone themself. The stone the road-singers touch for luck." The lute goes quiet. "I would touch it every spring. If it were you. Not today. Just: I would."

effects.log: "Then I will write it now," says {npc}, "so it is ready." {He} hums it all the way to the inn.

choices.text: Say the roads are not finished with you

effects.log: "No," says {npc}, "I can hear that." And {he} plays you to the next milestone.

events.text: {npc} stops at a crossing no map shows. "If you ever wanted to stop walking," {he} says, "this is where. The last milestone. Nobody would find it but me." {He} does not say it lightly. "I would come every spring. That is the verse. That is all of it."

choices.text: Tell {him} you will remember the place

effects.log: {npc} ties a red thread on a bush by the crossing, for finding it again. You both pretend it is for luck.
"Because somebody should sing to a milestone," says {npc}. "Even one that used to be greedy." It is said kindly. You walk on lighter.

events.text: Ding! [A SCHOOL MAY BE FOUNDED.] The System shows you a muddy yard by the ferry and a roof that leaks. A ferry-hand's child with a pole taller than {him} is already there, swinging it at reeds. {npc}. "Are you a teacher?" {he} asks. "My mother says teachers cost money. I have a fish."

choices.text: Take the fish, and the pupil

effects.log: {npc} bows so low the pole hits the mud. The System, very quietly, writes a name in a book that has no other names in it yet.
"Nothing is too much," says {npc}, and leaves the fish on the step anyway. You eat it, and teach {him} a stance.

choices.text: Ask who taught the ferry folk before

effects.log: "The god did," says {npc}. "My grandmother says the god of {b10_world} showed the first ferryman how to stand in a boat." You know, oddly, which foot goes first.

events.text: {npc}, the ferry-hand's child, stops swinging the pole. "My grandmother says there was a school here once," {he} says. "By the ferry. Its teacher had a way of standing like yours. When the teacher left, the school stood on its own a hundred years." {He} looks at the mud. "I would like to be in a school like that."

effects.log: "Promise?" says {npc}. You do. The System writes the first name in the book, and underlines it.
You show {him} a stance you have never learned. {npc} copies it perfectly on the first try, as if the mud remembered.

events.text: Word gets round the river towns. A dozen children come to the ferry, and one of them is the miller's son, strong and quick and rich. The Millrace School up the river has offered for the boy too. "You could take the boy and win every match on the river," says {npc}, "or you could take the ones nobody else wants. Like me."

effects.log: The yard fills with children who cannot afford a fish between them. {npc} teaches the youngest how to fall. The System appraises them one by one, and is surprised by every one.

choices.text: Take the miller's son and the strongest few

effects.log: The yard is smaller and better. The miller pays well. {npc} stands at the edge of it with {his} pole and watches the others walk home.

events.text: The Millrace School sends a challenge downriver: a match on the landing, three bouts, at the harvest fair. Their teacher, Bram Holloway, is a big friendly man who has never lost. {npc} has been practising for weeks. "Let me fight the first bout," {he} says. "Please."

effects.log: {npc} loses the first bout, and gets up, and bows, and the crowd cheers louder than for the win. Bram Holloway shakes {his} hand.

choices.text: Send your best and fight to win

ok.log: Your best take two bouts of three and the landing roars. Bram Holloway laughs and pays the purse. {npc} cheers from the back, not picked.

fail.log: Your best lose all three, cleanly. Bram Holloway is very kind about it, which is worse. {npc} says nothing, which is worst.

events.text: A school of anyone is a school of no money. The roof leaks onto the practice yard and the children train in puddles. {npc} has started teaching the little ones when you are away, badly and with great love. "We need a hall," {he} says. "A real one. With a roof."

choices.text: Spend your savings on the hall

effects.log: A practice hall goes up by the landing with a roof that does not leak. The children sleep in it the first night out of pure joy.

choices.text: Build it with the ferry folk, plank by plank

effects.log: It takes a whole summer and half the river towns. When it is done it leans a little, and everyone who built it loves it.

events.text: The small strong school wins and wins. One wet morning {npc} is gone, and so is {his} pole. A ferry child says {he} took the boat to the Millrace School. "Said {he} was only ever going to stand at the edge," the child says. "Said the Millrace takes anybody."

effects.log: You find {npc} on the Millrace landing, sweeping. You ask {him} to come back. {He} says {he} will think about it, which is more than you deserve.
You let {him} go. The school wins the next match too. The System appraises your pupils, and finds them all exactly as gifted as before.

events.text: Ding. The System appraises a pupil at the ferry school: a silent girl called Nell who carries baskets for the fishwives. [HIDDEN GIFT: the Ferryman's Luck.] Nell has never won a bout. {npc} watches you read Nell and asks quietly, "Does the System say what it reads in me?"

choices.text: Tell {him} the truth: it reads patience

effects.log: "Is that a gift?" says {npc}. "The best one," you say. {He} goes red to the ears and practises twice as long.

choices.text: Put Nell in the next match

effects.log: Nell wins a first bout by stepping out of the way at exactly the right moment, three times. The landing laughs, then cheers.

choices.text: Say the System reads what it reads

effects.log: {npc} nods and goes back to the pole. Some answers are only words.

events.text: Ding! The school by the ferry has met its fourth goal. The children line up on the landing at dawn, puddles and all, and bow to the river first and to you second, which is how {npc} taught them. The System reads the whole yard at once. [EVERY PUPIL HERE HAS A GIFT. SO DID THE FIRST.] {npc} is at the end of the line, holding the pole.

effects.log: You bow to a yard of children who could not afford a fish. The river, somehow, bows too.
{npc} drops the pole. Then picks it up, and stands straighter than you have ever seen {him} stand.

events.text: Ding! The school by the ferry has met its fourth goal: a match won against the Millrace on their own landing. At the edge of the crowd, in a Millrace sash, stands {npc}. {He} claps with everyone else. The System, reading the yard, pauses on {him}. [A GIFT WAS HERE. IT WAS LET GO.]

effects.log: {npc} bows back. Neither of you says sorry. Both of you mean it.

choices.text: Ask Bram Holloway how {he} is doing

effects.log: "Best pupil I have," says Bram. "Patient. Teaches the little ones when I am away. Learned that somewhere."

events.text: {npc} sits on the landing with you at dusk, grown now, the pole across {his} knees. "The school could stand without you," {he} says carefully. "If you ever wanted. You could be the lamp on the landing. The light we bow to when we cross." {He} looks at the water. "I am not asking. I only wanted you to know we would keep it lit."

effects.log: {npc} nods, and leans {his} shoulder against yours, the way {he} did when {he} was small and the boat rocked.

choices.text: Say there is still teaching to do

effects.log: "There always is," says {npc}, and goes to shout at the little ones about their feet.

events.text: {npc} comes down from the Millrace with the dawn ferry and sits by you on the landing. "I would come back," {he} says, "if the school ever needed a keeper. If you went on. Became the lamp on the landing, or whatever teachers become." {He} turns the pole in {his} hands. "I ran once. I would not run again."

choices.text: Say you would give it to {him}

effects.log: {npc} looks at you a long time. "Then I had better learn to deserve it," {he} says, and takes the ferry back to the Millrace to finish learning.
"So am I," says {npc}. The ferry waits for {him}, which it never does for anyone.

events.text: At the harvest fair of {pw_kingdom} a broad-shouldered master spins a threshing flail in the fair yard: the Thresher's Turn, round and round, and the crowd ducks. Ding. The Mirror flickers behind your eyes. [ONE MORE LOOK.] The master stops and stares straight at you over the crowd. {npc}. "You," {he} says. "You are watching wrong. You are watching like a thief."

effects.log: "Kesh Stone," {he} says, "of the Lowfield yards." {He} spins the Turn once more, slowly, on purpose. "If you are going to steal, steal it properly."
You are gone before {npc} reaches the rope. The Mirror holds half a form, and {he} holds your face.

choices.text: Ask where the form came from

effects.log: "The god of {b10_world} turned the first sheaf," says {npc}. "Every child in the Lowfields knows that." The Mirror, for no reason, goes warm.

events.text: {npc}, a fair-yard master of the Lowfields, sees you watching and lowers the flail. "My teacher's teacher had a story," {he} says. "A watcher at the fairs, who copied every form of the yards and gave them all back better." {He} looks at your eyes. "Said you could tell them by how they looked at a form. Like they had seen it first."

effects.log: "Then look properly," says {npc}, and spins the Thresher's Turn for you alone, slow as honey.

choices.text: Say it was only a story

effects.log: "They always are," says {npc}. {He} does not believe you, and does not hold it against you.

events.text: The Mirror holds the Thresher's Turn now, whole and clean, and at the next fair you use it in a match and win. In the crowd {npc} stands very still. Afterwards {he} finds you behind the cattle pens. "That is my turn," {he} says. "Twelve years I built it. You watched it twice."

choices.text: Tell {him} the truth and ask to be taught

effects.log: You tell {npc} about the Mirror. {He} is silent for a long time. "Twice," {he} says at last. "Fine. Then you will learn the other ten years from me."

choices.text: Say a form belongs to whoever can do it

effects.log: {npc} looks at you the way the Lowfields look at a hailstorm. "Then I will see you in every yard of the kingdoms," {he} says, "and we will find out who can do it."

events.text: At the Drovers' fair the Mirror catches another master, an old woman with a stick, and starts copying before you can stop it. {npc} is there, watching you watch. "That is my mother," {he} says. "My mother is seventy. That stick is the only thing my mother owns that is made by hand."

choices.text: Close your eyes until the old woman is done

effects.log: You stand in the fair yard with your eyes shut, and the Mirror sulks. The old woman finishes and bows. {npc} bows to you, very slightly.
The Mirror takes the Drover's Stick whole. The old woman does not know. {npc} does.

events.text: Learning properly takes years. {npc} is a hard teacher: you spin the flail in the Lowfield mud until your arms shake, and {he} says only "Again." The Mirror grumbles that it already has the form. {npc} hears you laugh at something and asks what. "The Mirror says it knows this already," you say.

effects.log: "It knows the shape," says {npc}. "You will know the weight." By autumn you do, and the Mirror is quiet.

choices.text: Ask {him} to teach you the Netcaster's Throw too

effects.log: {npc} grins. "Greedy," {he} says. "Good." {He} takes you to the coast fairs.

events.text: {npc} keeps the promise. At every fair yard of the kingdoms there is {npc}, rope-side, waiting. Every match you win with a copied form {he} answers with the real one, and some of them you lose. Word goes round: the thief and the Lowfield master.

choices.text: Beat {him} in front of the whole fair

ok.log: You beat {npc} with {his} own Turn, and the crowd goes wild. {He} gets up out of the straw and says, "Again," and means it.

fail.log: {npc} turns the real Turn, and your copy comes apart in the middle. You lie in the straw and look at the sky while the fair laughs.

choices.text: Offer {him} a form of yours for one of {his}

effects.log: {npc} stares at you over the rope. Then, slowly, {he} holds out a hand.

events.text: At the coast fair a net-maker named Lio throws a fishing net in the yard so wide it covers the crowd like a sky: the Netcaster's Throw. The Mirror leans forward. {npc} leans on the rope beside you. "Well?" {he} says. "Are you going to ask Lio, or just look?"

effects.log: Lio laughs and hands you a net. It takes a week and a great deal of seaweed. The Mirror, for once, has to wait its turn.
The Mirror takes the Throw in one long look. Lio never knows. {npc} knows, and sighs.
You watch the net open over the crowd like a flower. Some things are better not kept.

events.text: Ding! [THREE FORMS OF THE FAIR YARDS.] At the great fair of {pw_kingdom} the Mirror shows you all of them at once, and under them something older: the first form of all, a turn of a sheaf in a field before there were fairs. Your own hand turned it. {npc} stands in the yard with the flail. "Show me," {he} says. "Whatever you are looking at. Show me."

effects.log: You turn it, slow, and {npc} turns it back, and the fair yard goes quiet as a field. Neither of you made it. Both of you did.

choices.text: Show {him} {his} own Turn, as the Mirror keeps it

effects.log: {npc} watches {his} twelve years come out of your hands. "Huh," {he} says. "It is better than I thought."

events.text: Ding! The Mirror is full of the fair yards, and it hums. {npc} finds you at the empty fairground after dark. "I have watched you copy half the masters of the kingdoms," {he} says. "Tell me one thing. When you look at a form like that, what do you see?" The Mirror answers before you can. [THE ONE WHO TAUGHT THEM ALL.]

effects.log: {npc} is quiet a long while. "Then it was never stealing," {he} says slowly. "It was looking at your own handwriting."

choices.text: Say you see a fight worth having

effects.log: {npc} laughs, short and surprised, and picks up the flail. You fight till dawn and nobody wins.

events.text: {npc} walks the empty fair yard with you. "The Mirror has every form we have," {he} says. "It could give the last one away. Yours. To every yard in the world, so every child learns one form nobody remembers inventing." {He} spins the flail once. "I would teach it. If it came to that. Not today."

effects.log: "Then I will learn it properly first," says {npc}. "Twice is not enough."

choices.text: Spin the Turn with {him} once more

effects.log: You spin it together, and the empty yard sounds like threshing.

events.text: {npc} meets you on the last fair road of the year. "I have thought about the Mirror," {he} says. "You could close it. Step inside and shut it, and every master in the kingdoms would keep their own forms again, and teach them how they liked." {He} looks at the ground. "I would teach mine for free. If you did that."

choices.text: Say you will think of the masters

effects.log: {npc} nods once. It is the nearest {he} has come to forgiving you, and you both know it.

choices.text: Ask if {he} would miss the fights

effects.log: "Every day," says {npc}. "Do not tell anyone."

events.text: [LEVEL UP.] Then, for the first time: [LEVEL CAP REACHED SOON. THIS WORLD IS SMALL.] In an inn of {pw_kingdom} a lanky stranger at the next table looks up sharply, as if {he} had heard it too. {npc}. "You get the windows," {he} says, low. "The square ones. So do I. I hit the ceiling here years ago." {He} holds up a hand flat over {his} head. "This world only goes so high."
events.arc: The Level Cap of a Small World

effects.log: "Badly, at first," says {npc}. "Then I started fixing roofs." {He} buys you a cup and tells you about the ceiling.

choices.text: Ask why the world is so small

effects.log: "Its god made it small," says {npc}. "Folk say the god of {b10_world} made it a little at a time, like a garden." You feel, oddly, defensive about the garden.

choices.text: Say you will break the ceiling alone

effects.log: {npc} smiles without much hope. "Everybody says that," {he} says, and pays for your cup.

events.text: {npc}, a Player of {b10_world}, stares at the window over your head. "There was one before me," {he} says. "Broke the ceiling of this world. The whole world went up a level after." {He} rubs {his} eyes. "I read about it in the annals. The annals did not say who. Your window has the same border. Gold at the corners."
events.arc: The Level Cap of a Small World

effects.log: "Then you know the way," says {npc}, and {his} window, for the first time in years, shows a little experience bar moving.
[REMEMBERED: THE WORLD ROSE ONCE BEFORE.] You do not tell {npc}. You do not need to. {He} saw the window too.

events.text: {npc} shows you how the ceiling moves. "The world's faith," {he} says. "Build a bridge, end a feud, dig a well, and the people trust the world a little more, and the ceiling lifts. Slowly." {He} points at the hills, where bandits camp. "Or you can hunt those for experience until you hit the ceiling, and push. That works too. It hurts."
events.arc: The Level Cap of a Small World

effects.log: You dig a well for a hill village with {npc} holding the rope. [THE WORLD TRUSTS ITSELF A LITTLE MORE.] The ceiling creaks.
You hunt the hills for a season. The numbers climb fast, and the ceiling comes down to meet you like a low door. {npc} winces every time you hit it.

events.text: A bridge on the river road is down, and a whole kingdom's carts are stuck on the far bank. {npc} is already wading out with a plank. "This is worth more than a hundred bandits," {he} calls. "To the ceiling, I mean." On the bank a cart-boss offers you good money to fight off the hill gangs instead.
events.arc: The Level Cap of a Small World

choices.text: Wade out and build the bridge

effects.log: It takes a month and every cart-hand on both banks. When it is done the window says [THE WORLD RISES A LITTLE.] {npc} is soaked and grinning.

choices.text: Take the cart-boss's money and fight

effects.log: You drive off the hill gangs and the cart-boss pays well. The experience is good. The bridge is still down.

events.text: Deeds are slow. A year of wells and bridges and the ceiling has lifted barely a hand's width. Players who hunt pass you on the road. {npc} sits with you on a half-built wall. "I used to count," {he} says. "Then I counted the people who drank from the well instead. That number is better."
events.arc: The Level Cap of a Small World

effects.log: Three hundred and twelve people, and a goat. The window says nothing, but the ceiling, when you look, has moved.

choices.text: Pay for a mill for the village

effects.log: The mill turns by spring. [THE WORLD TRUSTS ITSELF A LITTLE MORE.] The village names the millpond after you, which is embarrassing.

events.text: The ceiling is a real thing now. Every time you reach it the window flashes red and something presses down on your head like a hand. [CANNOT EXCEED THE WORLD.] {npc} finds you sitting in the road with a nosebleed. "I did that for three years," {he} says. "It does not get softer. You just get stubborner."
events.arc: The Level Cap of a Small World

ok.log: You push and the ceiling gives a hair. [+1 TO THE WORLD.] {npc} stares. "Nobody has ever moved it that way," {he} says, a little frightened.

fail.log: The ceiling does not move. You do, backwards, into the ditch.

choices.text: Let {him} take you to fix a roof instead

effects.log: You fix a roof in silence. The window, for once, does not flash red. It says, quietly, [+1 TRUST].

events.text: A girl in the hill village has a window too, a tiny one with a cracked border. [LEVEL 1. CAP 1.] The girl does not know what it means. The girl's name is Wenna. {npc} looks at you over the child's head. "The ceiling is lowest for the new ones," {he} says. "It is the world's ceiling. Not ours."
events.arc: The Level Cap of a Small World

choices.text: Teach Wenna how the ceiling moves

effects.log: You teach Wenna to dig a well. The window says [CAP 2] by autumn, and Wenna cries with joy over the number two.

choices.text: Tell Wenna the window is a friend

effects.log: Wenna pats the window as if it were a dog. It glows, a little.

choices.text: Give Wenna's family a season's money

effects.log: Wenna's family eats well all winter. The window does not change. Wenna's face does.

events.text: [THE WORLD'S CEILING BREAKS.] It happens on an ordinary morning. Every window in {b10_world} flickers at once: yours, {npc}'s, Wenna's in the hills, others you never knew. Then the windows say together: [LEVEL CAP RAISED.] {npc} sits down in the road and laughs until {he} cries. "You lifted the whole thing," {he} says. "All of us."
events.arc: The Level Cap of a Small World

choices.text: Sit down in the road with {him}

effects.log: You laugh together in the road while carts go round you. The window says nothing at all, and that is right.

choices.text: Look up at where the ceiling was

effects.log: Above you is only sky. You made it once, at this height, on purpose. Now it is higher.

events.text: [THE CEILING BREAKS.] You push and it gives, and you go through it like a diver through ice, and on the other side there is nothing pressing down at all. {npc} is beside you, bloody-nosed too, because {he} pushed with you. "Huh," {he} says. "It breaks for two. Who knew."
events.arc: The Level Cap of a Small World

effects.log: "Do not thank me," says {npc}. "I have been waiting nine years for a second pair of hands."
You push and there is nothing to push against. [NO CEILING FOUND.] It is the loneliest window you have ever seen.

events.text: {npc} shows you a window you have not seen before. It has only one line. [RAISE THE WORLD: ALL YOUR LEVELS.] "It came after the ceiling broke," {he} says. "You could give everything you have to the world, and the world would rise, and so would they." {He} closes it. "I am not saying do it. I am saying it is there."
events.arc: The Level Cap of a Small World

choices.text: Say you will keep it in mind

effects.log: "Keep it in mind with a friend nearby," says {npc}. "That is all I ask."
"Fix one more roof first," says {npc}. "Always one more roof."

events.text: {npc} walks you up the hill road at dusk. "If you ever press that last window," {he} says, "the one that gives the world your levels, I want to be beside you. Pushing. The way we broke the ceiling." {He} kicks a stone. "I did not have anyone for nine years. You should not go up into the numbers alone."
events.arc: The Level Cap of a Small World

effects.log: {npc} nods and does not say anything for a mile, which for {npc} is a speech.

choices.text: Say the world is lucky to have {him}

effects.log: "The world does not know I exist," says {npc}. "That is fine. You do."

events.text: On a roof in {pw_kingdom} a stargazer with ink on {his} fingers is mapping the sky with a brass tube. {npc}. "That one," {he} says, pointing at the brightest, "the people call the Maker's Lamp. The god of {b10_world} hung it first." The star flickers. Something behind your eyes says, very kindly: [THE LAMP IS WATCHING YOU.] "It just winked," {npc} says. "It never winks."

choices.text: Ask {him} to teach you the stars

effects.log: {npc} teaches you seven before dawn. Each one you name glows a little, as if it had heard its name from an old friend.
"The almanacs say each star has a taste," says {npc}. "Kindness, or courage, or a good joke. The god gave them their tastes." You find you know which star likes jokes.
You wave. The Lamp, unmistakably, brightens. {npc} drops the brass tube off the roof.

events.text: {npc}, a stargazer, turns {his} brass tube from the sky to you and back. "My almanac has a page about a person the stars loved," {he} says. "They all turned to watch, the night that person was born. The page is very old." {He} looks up. "They have all turned now. Toward this roof."

choices.text: Tell {him} the stars are old friends

effects.log: {npc} believes you at once, which almost nobody would. {He} writes it in the almanac, under the old page.
You look up at the stars you set, and they look down at the soul that set them. It is very quiet on the roof.

events.text: {npc} has worked out the stars' tastes from three hundred years of almanacs. "The Lamp likes kindness to strangers," {he} says. "The red one likes courage. The faint one likes a long life well kept." {He} taps the page. "Live the way they like and they warm to you. Or," {he} adds, "you could go up to the high hill and ask the Lamp what it wants. Nobody ever has."

effects.log: You give a stranger your coat that winter, and the Lamp warms. {npc} logs it, delighted: "Pleased, the third night of frost."

choices.text: Climb the high hill and ask

effects.log: You climb all night. At the top the Lamp says, in your own voice: [YOU GAVE ME MY TASTES. WHY ASK ME?] {npc}, puffing behind you, writes that down with shaking hands.

events.text: The red star, the one that likes courage, burns very bright over a village where the river has burst. {npc} hands you the brass tube. "It wants to see someone brave," {he} says. "Or it is only bright. Almanacs are not certain." Below, a family is on a roof with the water rising.

effects.log: You bring the family down one at a time. The red star blazes. {npc} waits on the bank with blankets and the almanac, writing with wet hands.

choices.text: Tell the star to want something else

effects.log: You shout at a star. The village wades out by itself. The red star flickers, as if it were thinking it over. {npc} stares at you.

events.text: Living to the stars' tastes is not easy. The Lamp likes kindness to strangers, and strangers are not always kind back. You are robbed twice on the road by people you fed. {npc} binds your hand on the roof. "The almanac says the Lamp likes it best when it costs," {he} says. "I think the almanac was written by someone who never paid."

effects.log: You do. The Lamp burns so bright that night that the almanac-makers of three kingdoms write it down.
You laugh on the roof until the stars seem to laugh too.

events.text: The stars do not like being argued with. For a season they go cold over your roof, all of them, and the almanacs of the kingdoms record a strange dark patch over one town. {npc} keeps watching anyway. "You told them what to like once," {he} says. "Maybe they want to tell you something back."

effects.log: You lie on the roof and listen. The faint star says, very quietly: [WE LIKED WHAT YOU GAVE US. WE ONLY WANTED TO BE ASKED.] The roof is warm all night.

ok.log: You argue all night, and at dawn the Lamp laughs, your old laugh, and warms. [YOU ALWAYS DID WIN THESE.] It sounds pleased to have lost.

fail.log: The Lamp is silent. You lose an argument with your own star, which is a lesson of a kind.

events.text: One of the stars is new to {npc}'s almanacs, and it is the star of a world you finished as a god, long ago. Its light is tired and fond. {npc} has named it in pencil: "the Old Friend." "It likes long walks," {he} says. "I cannot tell you how I know. I just do."

choices.text: Take a long walk under it

effects.log: You walk all night under the Old Friend. It follows you like a dog. In the morning there is money in your boot that you did not put there.
{npc} writes it all down: a sea of glass, a people who sang. "I will put it in the almanac," {he} says. "As a story. Nobody will believe it."

events.text: Ding! [FIVE TIMES THE STARS HAVE BEEN PLEASED.] That night every star over {b10_world} turns, and the Maker's Lamp comes down the sky a little, low enough that its light lies on the roof like a blanket. It speaks in your old voice. [WELCOME HOME. WE KEPT YOUR SKY.] {npc} has stopped writing. {He} is crying, quietly, into the almanac.

effects.log: The stars glow. The Lamp goes back up, slowly, the way a parent leaves a sleeping child.

choices.text: Ask {him} to write it all down

effects.log: {npc} writes until dawn. It is the best page of the almanac, and nobody will believe a word of it.

events.text: Ding! [THE STARS ARE PLEASED.] They are pleased, the Lamp says, not because you did what they liked, but because you argued with them like the one who made them. The sky over {b10_world} rearranges itself for one hour into the shape of your hand. {npc} sits frozen with the brass tube. "That," {he} says, "is not in any almanac."

effects.log: The sky waves back. Somewhere, the almanac-makers of three kingdoms all drop their pens at once.

choices.text: Ask the oldest star to stay close

effects.log: The Lamp settles a finger-width lower in the sky, and stays there. {npc} will spend years explaining it.

events.text: {npc} rolls up the almanac on the roof. "There is a new page," {he} says. "For a star that is not up there yet. The almanac says a person could go up among the stars they set. Be a new light over the world they made." {He} ties the scroll. "I would name it. If it were you. Not tonight."

effects.log: {npc} tells you. It is a very good name. You keep it to yourself, as a present for later.

choices.text: Say tonight there are still strangers to feed

effects.log: "There always are," says {npc}, and hands you a loaf for the road.

events.text: {npc} points the brass tube at the Lamp. "The oldest star in the sky," {he} says. "If you ever went up, I think you would go beside it. The two of you would argue for a thousand years over the river towns." {He} smiles. "I would watch every night. I would write down who won."

effects.log: "I will write that down too," says {npc}. "In pencil."
"Then nobody wins," says {npc}, "and I get to watch forever." It sounds like {he} has thought about it.

events.text: The notebook's first page is in your own hand. [IN THE THIRD YEAR, THE LOWER TOWNS OF {pw_kingdom} WILL FLOOD.] In the archive of {pw_kingdom} a chronicler with dust in {his} hair is copying the annals by lamplight. {npc}. "The annals of {b10_world}," {he} says, "begin with the god making the first river. After that it is mostly floods." {He} looks at your notebook. "What do you have there?"
events.arc: The Guide of a Mortal Life There

effects.log: {npc} reads it twice and goes pale. "That is next spring," {he} says. "How do you know about next spring?"

choices.text: Say it is only a diary

effects.log: {npc} nods politely and writes something in the margin of the annals. You never see what.

choices.text: Ask who wrote the first annal

effects.log: "The god, they say," says {npc}. "In water, on the first bank." The notebook in your hands is very slightly damp.

events.text: {npc}, a chronicler of {b10_world}, pulls down a volume from the high shelf. "There is an annal," {he} says, "of a stranger who knew the years ahead. Warned the towns of every flood. Corrected the annals before they were written." {He} blows the dust off. "The hand in the margin looks like the hand in your notebook."
events.arc: The Guide of a Mortal Life There

effects.log: "Then you can help me with next spring," says {npc}, and pulls up a second chair.
In the margin, in your hand: [THE CHRONICLER WILL BE KIND. LET THEM.] You close the book.

events.text: The flood tip is true; you can feel it in the notebook like cold water. {npc} spreads the map of the lower towns on the archive table. "If we warn them," {he} says, "the annals will say we were mad until the water comes. If you keep it quiet, you could buy the high ground now, cheap, and sell it after."
events.arc: The Guide of a Mortal Life There

effects.log: You and {npc} ride from town to town with the notebook. Most laugh. Some move. When the water comes, the ones who moved are dry.
The high ground is cheap and the flood is exactly on time. You sell dry fields to wet people at a good price. {npc} writes it in the annals without comment.

events.text: [UNDER THE OLD WELL OF THE MARKET SQUARE THERE IS SOMETHING THE SHADOW LODGES WANT.] {npc} reads the tip over your shoulder. "The Shadow Lodges," {he} says, very quietly. "The dark order. If they want it, it is either treasure or trouble." {He} looks at you. "Tell the Wardens of the League? Or go down yourself?"
events.arc: The Guide of a Mortal Life There

choices.text: Take it to the League's Wardens

effects.log: The Wardens dig up the well at night and find a chest of old maps the Lodges wanted badly. {npc} copies them all before they are carried off.
Under the well is a chest of old maps, worth a great deal to the right buyer. You keep them. The Shadow Lodges, somewhere, notice the well is empty.

events.text: Warning people is thankless. For every town that listens, two call you a crow. {npc} has started writing your warnings into the annals before they come true, so that afterwards nobody can say they were not told. "My colleagues think I have lost my mind," {he} says, cheerful. "I have never enjoyed the annals more."
events.arc: The Guide of a Mortal Life There

effects.log: A town on the river moves its granary uphill on your word. The next spring, it is the only granary that is not soup.
You sit up with {npc} copying until the lamp burns low. It is the best night of the year.

events.text: The tips pay. You have money, land, a name in the market. But the Shadow Lodges have noticed someone always knows first, and one night a grey-cloaked woman leaves a black feather on your door: an invitation. {npc} finds it in the morning. "They want you," {he} says. "People they want, they do not let go."
events.arc: The Guide of a Mortal Life There

choices.text: Burn the feather and go to the Wardens

effects.log: You burn it and tell the League everything. The Lodges go quiet. {npc} sleeps on your floor for a month anyway, just in case.

choices.text: Meet the Lodge and talk your way out

ok.log: You meet the grey-cloaked woman and talk until dawn, and when you leave the woman lets you go. The Lodge seemed amused. That is worse than angry.

fail.log: The talk goes badly. You leave by a window, and a Lodge knife leaves with you, in your arm.

events.text: [IN THE FIFTH YEAR, A LORD OF {pw_kingdom} WILL SELL THE KING TO THE SHADOW LODGES.] The tip is in your hand, but something about the ink is wrong. It smells of the Lodges' own grey candles. {npc} turns the page to the light. "Is it true?" {he} asks. "You always know, somehow."
events.arc: The Guide of a Mortal Life There

choices.text: Trust the feeling, and test it

effects.log: You watch the lord for a month. The lord is only a dull man who loves dogs. [THE TIP WAS WRONG.] Someone wanted you to think so.

choices.text: Ask {him} what the annals say of the lord

effects.log: "Married, dull, owns forty dogs," says {npc}. "If the lord is a traitor, it is a very patient treason."

choices.text: Take it to the king anyway

effects.log: The king thanks you and does nothing, which was wise. The lord sends you a puppy, which is confusing.

events.text: Ding! [THREE TIPS HEEDED, THREE TIPS TRUE.] The notebook glows on the archive table. Every page fills at once with the years of {b10_world} ahead, and they are all corrected: the floods marked with warnings, the wells marked with wardens. {npc} reads the last line and laughs aloud. [THE CHRONICLER WAS RIGHT TO BELIEVE YOU.]
events.arc: The Guide of a Mortal Life There

effects.log: {npc} reads all night. In the morning {his} own annals have the same corrections in them, in {his} own hand.
It says, in your hand, a long time ago: [THANK THEM.] So you do.

events.text: Ding! [THREE TIPS HEEDED, THREE TIPS TRUE.] The notebook glows, and the years ahead come clear, and you see at last who wrote it: a god, once, writing down the floods it had not stopped, so that someone might. Your hand. {npc} reads over your shoulder. "You were saving them for yourself," {he} says, without anger. "They were for everyone."
events.arc: The Guide of a Mortal Life There

effects.log: {npc} closes the notebook gently. "Then there is still time," {he} says. "There always is, in the annals."

choices.text: Say every god keeps a few

effects.log: {npc} writes that in the annals, word for word. It reads worse in ink.

events.text: {npc} sets the notebook beside the annals on the high shelf. "The notebook knows the rest of this world's years," {he} says. "You could write yourself into the annals, and close the book. Be part of the record. The last true entry." {He} brushes the spine. "I would keep it here. Up high. Where the damp cannot reach."
events.arc: The Guide of a Mortal Life There

choices.text: Say there are still years to warn

effects.log: "Then I will keep the lamp trimmed," says {npc}, and pulls up your chair.

choices.text: Ask what {he} would write about you

effects.log: "That you were right, mostly," says {npc}. "And kind, always. In that order, so nobody thinks I am soft."

events.text: {npc} turns {his} pen over and over. "If you closed the annals," {he} says, "I would want you to give me the pen first. So the world could write its own years afterwards. Not the notebook's. Ours." {He} looks at you. "I do not mean it unkindly. I mean it is our turn."
events.arc: The Guide of a Mortal Life There

effects.log: {npc} bows over the annals, and does not look up for a long while.

choices.text: Say the world writes its own years already

effects.log: "Then it writes badly," says {npc}, "and I will correct it." That is a chronicler's love.

events.text: Ding. [SIMULATE A LIFE?] On the market road of {pw_kingdom} someone under a patched awning lays out cards painted with ferries and fields. {npc}, a fortune-teller. "You have a loom behind your eyes," {he} says, without looking up. "I can always tell. Show me a small life, and I will tell you what it costs."

effects.log: You glimpse a life where you ran a ferry for forty years and never left the river. {npc} reads it on your face. "Happy," {he} says. "Small and happy. That costs nothing."
"The god of {b10_world} drew the first deck," says {npc}. "Every fortune-teller says so." The ferry card in your hand is, somehow, your old handwriting.

choices.text: Ask the price of a reading

effects.log: "For you, a coin," says {npc}. "For a god, more." {He} winks. You do not know why your heart jumps.

events.text: {npc}, the fortune-teller of the market road, turns over a card {he} has never turned before. It shows a figure at a loom weaving small lives. "My grandmother's deck," {he} says. "This card only turns for one kind of person. The last one wove a loom of their own and left it behind." {He} looks up. "Your hands look like the card."

effects.log: "Then the loom has been waiting," says {npc}, and sets a glimpse out for you, free.
{npc} lets you. "Some cards like to be turned twice," {he} says. "They are patient."

events.text: A girl at {npc}'s awning wants to know whether to marry the potter. "I can read the cards," {npc} says to you quietly, "or you can glimpse it. The loom will show the whole of it." Then, lower: "It could show you your own marriage too. Who to choose. What it would cost."

choices.text: Glimpse the girl's life on the girl's behalf

effects.log: You glimpse it: the potter, a loud house, three children, a long kind life. You tell the girl. The girl runs off to find the potter. {npc} smiles.
You glimpse a marriage of your own: a market house, good years, a hard end. You keep it close. The girl leaves with only the cards.

events.text: War drums on the road: {pw_kingdom} is mustering. {npc} closes {his} awning early. "Every family on this road wants to know who comes home," {he} says. "I cannot tell them. You could. One glimpse each." {He} hesitates. "Or you could glimpse which side wins, and sell your stores to the winner."

effects.log: One by one you glimpse their sons and daughters coming home, or not. You tell them gently. {npc} holds their hands.
You glimpse the war: which side, which month. You sell your stores well. On the road the families wait at {npc}'s closed awning.

events.text: Glimpsing other people's lives is heavy work. You see the potter's girl old and happy. You see a ferryman drown in a life that is not this one. At night you dream other people's weddings. {npc} brings you tea at the awning. "The loom is not meant to be carried alone," {he} says. "Give me half."

effects.log: You tell {npc} about the ferryman. {He} listens without flinching, and the weight is lighter after.

choices.text: Glimpse a field at harvest, for rest

effects.log: A field at harvest, gold and loud with larks. Nobody dies in it. You sleep that night.

events.text: You glimpse for yourself, and you grow very good at choosing. Every road you take is the best one the loom showed. But the market road has noticed you are never surprised. {npc} lays out a card for you without asking. It is blank. "That is what the cards see when they look at you now," {he} says. "A life that has already been read."

effects.log: {npc} reads you without the loom. It takes an hour. You are surprised four times. {He} charges you double.

choices.text: Glimpse a life you would never choose

ok.log: You glimpse a life of a beggar on the river road, and in it you are kind to everyone, and loved. You did not choose that life. You learn from it anyway.

fail.log: The glimpse slides away from you, the loom too tired of being used.

events.text: A child with no name sleeps under {npc}'s awning: Pell, an orphan of the market road. {npc} feeds {him} on fortunes. "The loom has no thread for Pell," {npc} says. "I have looked. It is as if nobody wove one." {He} glances at you. "The god forgot some of them, I think. In a hurry."

effects.log: The loom finds a thread, thin as a hair: Pell, a baker. You tell {npc}. {He} apprentices Pell to a baker that week.
Pell shows you a game with pebbles. It is a very good game. You lose.
Pell eats well all winter. The loom, when you look, has started a thread on its own.

events.text: Ding! [THREE KINDS OF SMALL LIFE GLIMPSED.] The loom behind your eyes becomes a loom in front of you, real wood, on {npc}'s awning, with every small life of {b10_world} on it, in thread: ferries, harvests, marriages, wars. In the warp, very faint, is the hand that strung it first. "That is you," {npc} whispers. "Is it not."

effects.log: {npc} touches the warp. "Then you strung us well," {he} says. "Mostly."

choices.text: Run your hand along the threads

effects.log: The threads hum under your fingers, warm, a whole world of small lives. None of them knows you. All of them do.

events.text: Ding! [THREE KINDS OF SMALL LIFE GLIMPSED.] The loom stands on the market road, real wood, and every thread you glimpsed for yourself is a bright knot on it. Around the knots the other threads are thin. {npc} sees it too. "You have been weaving only your own," {he} says, gently. "It is a beautiful knot. It is a lonely one."

choices.text: Ask {him} to help you unpick it

effects.log: You and {npc} unpick a knot together, and the threads around it fatten, one by one, like rivers after rain.
You keep weaving. The knot grows. The loom, very slightly, leans toward it.

events.text: {npc} folds the awning at dusk. "There is one more thing the loom can do," {he} says. "You could unweave this life. Give its thread to someone who has none. Pell, or someone like Pell." {He} does not look at you. "They would grow up lucky. Not today. I only thought you should know it is there."

choices.text: Say you will keep it in mind

effects.log: "Keep me in mind too," says {npc}, and hands you a card with a ferry on it, for luck.
"Fortune-tellers know the ends of things," says {npc}. "That is the sad part of the job."

events.text: {npc} lays one card face-down on the awning. "If you ever unwove yourself," {he} says, "I would ask you to unweave into my loom. Into the readings. They would be kinder after. I have always wanted kinder readings." {He} taps the card. "That is not a fortune. It is a wish."

effects.log: It is the loom card. {npc} looks at it, and at you, and smiles a small sad smile.
"Only because I lie a little," says {npc}. "You would not need to."

events.text: [ROLE: VILLAIN.] At a river town fair a young farmhand catches a runaway cart one-handed, and everyone cheers. Ding. The System reads {him}: [BLESSED: LUCK OF THE MAKER, TWICE.] Your blessings, from when you were the god of {b10_world}. {npc}, a farmhand with a wide grin and a broken hat, waves at the crowd. "I am going to be a hero," {he} announces. "Somebody has to be."

effects.log: {npc} grins at you. "I have plenty," {he} says. You know. You gave it to {him}.
{npc} trips, and lands on a hay bale that was not there a moment ago. Your old blessings, doing their work.
"The god likes me," says {npc}, simply. "Always has." Somewhere a very old part of you says: yes.

events.text: {npc}, the luckiest farmhand in {pw_kingdom}, looks at you over a fence. "My grandmother told a story," {he} says, "about a dark lord who let the hero win, in the end. Took off the mask in the market square." {He} squints. "My grandmother said the dark lord stood like you. Are you a dark lord?"

effects.log: "Good," says {npc}. "Then I know how the story ends." {He} climbs the fence and shakes your hand.

choices.text: Say there is no such thing

effects.log: {npc} nods, unconvinced, and goes off whistling, and trips on nothing at all. [THE HERO'S LUCK: A LITTLE THINNER.] The System sounds smug.

events.text: {npc} has a sword now, a cloak, and a band of friends from the river towns, and the System has a plan. [STRIKE WHERE YOUR BLESSINGS LEFT A GAP.] You know where: {he} is only lucky in daylight. You blessed the sun, not the moon. "You could make {him} lose and learn," says the System. "Or just lose."

effects.log: You set a night trap that {npc} walks into and out of, humbled, with a sprained pride and a lesson about the dark. {He} trains at night after that.
You strike at {npc} by moonlight and {his} band scatters. {He} sits in the mud of the market road and does not understand why the luck ran out.

events.text: The river towns pay you tribute now, fearfully, a basket at the crossroads every month. In one basket is a letter from a child: please do not hurt the hero, {he} gave us {his} boots. {npc}'s boots are in the basket too. They are very worn.

choices.text: Send the boots back, and the basket too

effects.log: You send it all back with a note: the hero needs boots more than a dark lord does. {npc} reads it aloud in the square, puzzled.
You keep it. A dark lord must. {npc} walks barefoot that winter, and the river towns tell the story with you as the reason.

events.text: Being a villain with a code is lonely work. You lose more than you win, on purpose, and the System keeps grumbling about points. Your henchman, a retired goose-thief named Old Dabb, does not understand. "You keep letting the boy off," Dabb says. "What kind of dark lord does that?" {npc}, meanwhile, is getting very good.

choices.text: Tell Dabb it is a long story

effects.log: Dabb sighs and polishes your helmet. "Long stories are the best kind," Dabb says. You agree.

choices.text: Set the hero a harder trial

effects.log: {npc} climbs the cliff you set, shaking, and does not fall. {His} luck, for once, is not needed. The System grumbles: [LUCK THINNING.] {npc} does not notice. {He} is too busy being brave.

events.text: {npc} comes for you, angry now, with half the river towns behind {him}. The luck you gave {him} is thinner than it was and {he} knows it. "You took it," {he} says at your gate. "I do not know how. You took my luck."

ok.log: You win, and {npc} goes down in the gate-mud. {He} looks up at you with something new in {his} face: not fear. Understanding.

fail.log: Luck or no luck, {npc} is good now. You end up in your own moat, and the river towns cheer.

choices.text: Tell {him} the luck was yours to begin with

effects.log: {npc} stares. Then {he} laughs, an awful laugh. "Of course it was," {he} says, and goes home to think.

events.text: In the temple of the god of {b10_world} by the river, {npc} kneels and prays for strength to beat the dark lord. You stand at the back in a plain cloak. The prayer goes up, and you hear it, as you always would have. The old priest Lusk lights a candle for the hero.

effects.log: You let {npc} feel the god near. {He} gets up braver. It is the strangest thing a dark lord ever did.
Two candles, the hero's and the villain's, burn side by side in your own temple. Lusk does not ask.
You go. Behind you {npc} prays on, to a god who has just walked out the door.

events.text: Ding. [THREE SETBACKS.] The hero is humbled three times and still standing, and {npc} is not the lucky farmhand any more: {he} is a hero who knows the dark, because you taught {him}. The river towns pay you tribute so that you will not come, and {npc} rides out to tell them they need not. "I will handle the dark lord," {he} says. "I know the dark lord's habits."

effects.log: You let {npc} say it. The towns believe {him}. The System records: [VILLAIN: FEARED. HERO: TRUSTED.] It is the right way round.
{npc} reads your note in the square, and does not laugh. {He} keeps it.

events.text: Ding. [THREE SETBACKS.] {npc}'s luck is thin as river-ice, and the river towns are afraid of you in earnest. Tribute comes every month. {npc} stands outside your gate in the rain with no luck at all and a sword {he} has learned to use. "I am still coming," {he} says. "Without it. I am still coming."

effects.log: {npc} comes in, dripping. You talk all night by the fire, dark lord and hero, and agree on nothing but the tea.
You leave it shut. {npc} stands in the rain until dawn, and then goes home, and the System adds the points.

events.text: {npc} meets you on the river road, sword sheathed. "I have worked it out," {he} says. "You could take off the mask. Let me win, in the square, in front of everyone. Be the story their children hear." {He} scratches {his} head under the broken hat. "I would tell it well. With you at the end. Not today. Just: if you wanted."

effects.log: "Better than you would," says {npc}. "You would make yourself sound nice."

choices.text: Say the story is not finished

effects.log: "They never are," says {npc}, and rides on to the next town.

events.text: {npc}, older now, meets you on the river road. "If you ever let me win," {he} says, "I would ask one thing. Tell the story true. That you took the luck back. That I came anyway." {He} looks at you a long time. "It should be true. Even the dark lord's part."

effects.log: {npc} nods. "Mostly true," {he} says. "I will want to look a bit taller."

choices.text: Say the truth is not kind to you

effects.log: "No," says {npc}. "That is how I would know it was true."

events.text: The ring you found in the river is iron, plain, and warm. A voice in it says, rough as a millstone: "About time. I am Corran. I taught before there were kingdoms." At the river's edge a grey-haired stranger is staring at your hand. {npc}. "That is my teacher's ring," {he} says. "The teacher went into the river with it when I was a child. Is the teacher in there?"

effects.log: {npc} sits down on the riverbank very suddenly. "Tell the teacher," {he} says, "that I kept practising."
"My last pupil," says Corran. "Stubborn as a stone. Tell {him} nothing yet. Let {him} ask." The ring, you notice, is warmer.

choices.text: Close your hand and walk on

effects.log: You walk on with the ring. {npc} follows you three villages before {he} gives up.

events.text: {npc}, the grey-haired last pupil of an old master, catches your wrist on the river road. "My teacher said the ring would come back to the river," {he} says, "and that whoever carried it last would carry it again. Someone who had been a god once, my teacher said. I thought it a joke." From the ring, Corran says: "I was not."

effects.log: {npc} lets go of your wrist and bows, very low, to the ring and to you.

choices.text: Ask Corran for a lesson, now

effects.log: "Ha," says Corran. "Same as last time." Corran gives you one. The river remembers it.

events.text: Corran's first lesson is how the first people stood on a riverbank before there was a word for standing. "This art is older than every kingdom," Corran says. "Older than the god who made the world. Well. As old." {npc} watches you practise from a rock. "The teacher taught me half of it," {he} says. "The teacher went into the river before the other half."

effects.log: You teach {npc} each lesson as you learn it. Corran grumbles, then corrects {his} feet through you. {He} weeps, once, at a turn {he} had waited forty years for.
"{He} had {his} half," says Corran, unbothered. You practise alone. {npc} watches from the rock, and then stops coming.

events.text: A scholar of {pw_kingdom}'s court, Master Elwin, comes to the river. Elwin has heard of the ring. "An art from before the first kingdom," Elwin says, "belongs to the kingdom's library." {npc} stands beside you, fists closed. Corran, in the ring, laughs. "Before kingdoms means before libraries," Corran says.

choices.text: Tell Elwin it belongs to the river folk

effects.log: Elwin goes red, then laughs too, and asks only to write down the stories. {npc} tells them, all afternoon.
Elwin pays well for one lesson on paper. Corran is silent for a week. {npc} does not speak to you at all.

events.text: Teaching two is slower than learning one. Corran is impatient. {npc} is slow, and old, and stubborn. You spend more time between them than at the art. "Why do you bother?" Corran says one night. "{He} is old." "So are you," you say. The ring is quiet a long time.

effects.log: By spring {npc} has the turn Corran never taught {him}. Corran says nothing, and the ring is warm as bread.

choices.text: Ask Corran why the ring went into the river

effects.log: "Because a pupil must outgrow the teacher," says Corran, "and {he} would not while I was on the bank."

events.text: The art grows in you, strong and old, and you have no one to share it with. Corran is good company, but the ring is a voice in iron. You see {npc} on the river road one day, teaching children the half {he} has. Badly. With love. The ring says: "You could correct {his} feet."

effects.log: {npc} lets you, stiffly. By the end of the afternoon {he} is smiling and the children are standing like the first people.

choices.text: Test the art against a river bandit

ok.log: The old art moves through you like water, and the bandit sits down in the river, astonished. Corran laughs the millstone laugh.

fail.log: The old art is older than you are ready for. You end up in the river with the bandit, both of you very confused.

events.text: Corran tells you about the world before the first kingdom: the first fires, the first songs, and a god who walked among the first people and laughed at their jokes. "I taught the god a stance once," Corran says. "The god was very bad at it." Corran pauses. "You are also very bad at it." {npc} laughs on the bank, having heard it all before.

effects.log: Corran laughs too. It is a strange thing, to be teased by a man you once made.

choices.text: Practise it until you are not bad

effects.log: It takes a whole season. Corran says, at the end, grudgingly, "Better than the god."

choices.text: Ask what the god was like

effects.log: "Lonely," says Corran. "Made a whole world to have someone to talk to." You look at the ring for a long time.

events.text: Ding. [FIVE LESSONS.] The ring is hot as a forge, and Corran says: "That is all of it. The whole art from before the kingdoms. You and {npc} have it now. Nobody else." {npc} stands on the riverbank in the first stance there ever was, perfect, seventy years old and shaking with joy. "The teacher finished," {he} says. "The teacher finished teaching me."

effects.log: You bow to {npc} and to the ring. Corran, for once, has nothing rude to say.
Two of you on the bank, standing like the first people. The river slows down to look.

events.text: Ding. [FIVE LESSONS.] The ring burns, and the whole art from before the kingdoms is in your bones. Corran says: "All of it. To you alone. That is what you wanted." A pause. "Was it?" On the far bank {npc} is teaching children half a stance. From here you can see what {he} is missing, exactly.

effects.log: You cross. {npc} watches you come, and does not move away. You show {him} the rest, there, with the children watching.

choices.text: Keep the art whole in you

effects.log: "So be it," says Corran. The ring cools a little. The art, whole, is very heavy.

events.text: {npc} walks the riverbank with you, slow, the ring warm on your hand. "The ring has given you all it holds," {he} says. "You could lay it in the river again, with yourself in it, for the next child of this world to find. Like the teacher did." {He} glances at the water. "Not now. But I would know where to look."

choices.text: Tell {him} you will think of the next child

effects.log: "So did the teacher," says {npc}. "It took forty years. Take longer."

choices.text: Ask Corran what it is like in there

effects.log: "Quiet," says Corran. "Good company, now and then." Corran sounds content.

events.text: {npc} holds out {his} hand on the riverbank, palm up, old and steady. "If you go into the iron," {he} says, "do not go into the river. Give the ring to me. I will wear it on a cord. I would like to have someone to argue with, in my last years." From the ring Corran says: "{He} means me. And you. Both."

choices.text: Say you would give it to {him}

effects.log: {npc} closes {his} hand and nods once. It is a promise, of a kind.
"I always did," says {npc}. Corran, in the ring, does not disagree.

events.text: [FARMING 1/10.] A bar appears in the corner of your eye as you plant your first row. At the end of the field a broad figure with clay to the elbows and a guild-chain round the neck is watching. {npc}, guild-mother of the crafts of {pw_kingdom}. "You work like you are being counted," {he} says. "Are you?"

choices.text: Say yes, and show {him} the bar

effects.log: {npc} squints at the empty air where the bar is. "I cannot see it," {he} says. "But I believe it. Come to the guild."

choices.text: Ask who taught the first farmer

effects.log: "The god of {b10_world}," says {npc}. "Pressed the first seed in with a thumb." You look at your thumb. It is very good at seeds.
{npc} watches a full row, and leaves a guild-token on your fencepost. You leave it there.

events.text: {npc}, guild-mother of the kingdoms' crafts, runs a thumb along the bench where the masters stamp their marks. "There is a mark on this bench older than the guild," {he} says. "A master who turned gold in a craft and laid their tools down here. Nobody knows whose." {He} looks at your hands. "They held a hammer like you."

choices.text: Say it might have been you

effects.log: "Then you know the way to the bench," says {npc}. "Mind you take the long road again."
It is warm. [SMITHING +1.] The bar in your eye fills as if it remembered something.

events.text: The guild of {pw_kingdom} has rules: you learn under a master, you pay dues, you teach two apprentices before you may stamp your own mark. It is slow. A merchant of the river towns offers you a stall of your own, no guild, no dues, if you undercut the guild's prices by half. {npc} hears of it. "Your choice," {he} says. "It always is."

choices.text: Join the guild, dues and all

effects.log: {npc} puts you under old Tam the smith. It is slow and hot and Tam shouts. The bars fill steadily. {npc} drops by most weeks.
Your stall undercuts the whole street and the money pours in. The bars fill fast. {npc} walks past your stall without stopping.

events.text: A fever goes through the weavers' quarter, and the healers' guild is short of hands. {npc} comes to you in the evening, dusty and tired. "You have a healing bar," {he} says. "I know you do. The guild would let you work it here without dues. Or you could sell your herbs to the highest bidder. They are paying very high."

effects.log: You work the wards for a month. The healing bar fills with every night you sit up. Nobody dies of the fever who could have lived.
You sell well. The healing bar fills slowly; the purse fills fast. {npc} works the wards alone.

events.text: The guild is slow. Two apprentices before your own mark: a fishwife's son, Dov, who drops everything, and a quiet girl, Ama, who is better than you already at weaving. {npc} watches you teach them. "This is the craft too," {he} says. "Most masters forget."

choices.text: Teach Dov until the dropping stops

effects.log: It takes a year. Dov stops dropping things. The bar of smithing fills in a way it never did alone.
Ama is very patient with you. Your weaving bar jumps. So does your respect.

events.text: Your stall is the richest on the street, and the guild masters will not look at you. When your smithy roof catches fire, nobody from the guild comes. {npc} comes, alone, with a bucket. "I am not here for you," {he} says. "I am here for the street."

choices.text: Thank {him}, and ask how to make it right

effects.log: "Pay your dues," says {npc}. "Late. With interest. And teach someone." You do.

ok.log: You put it out with {npc}'s bucket and your own hands. {He} nods once. It is not forgiveness. It is a start.

fail.log: The fire takes the roof. You save the anvil, and burn your arm doing it.

events.text: At the trading fair of the kingdoms a rival guild-master, Hesk of the Saltmarsh, sets a challenge: whoever sells the most by sundown wins the fair's banner. {npc} raises an eyebrow at you. "Your trading bar is the lowest," {he} says. "This would fill it. Or empty you."

ok.log: You sell everything you brought and two things you did not. The banner is yours. Hesk shakes your hand and asks to buy your secret.

fail.log: Hesk sells more, and kindly. You learn a great deal about trading, mostly from losing.

effects.log: You watch Hesk all day. By sundown you understand trading better than a year of stalls taught you.
You and {npc} sell the guild's goods together, and lose to Hesk, and laugh about it all the way home.

events.text: Ding! [A BAR TURNS GOLD.] The guild of {pw_kingdom} meets in the old hall, and {npc} calls your name in front of every master of the kingdoms. "A known master," {he} says, and the masters stamp their feet on the boards, which is the guild's cheer. Dov and Ama stamp hardest. On the bench, the old mark nobody can read is warm.

choices.text: Stamp your mark beside the old one

effects.log: Your mark goes on the bench beside the old one. They look, the masters say afterwards, like the same hand.
Dov drops the hammer in surprise. Ama laughs. {npc} nods: that is the craft too.

events.text: Ding! [A BAR TURNS GOLD.] You are a master, gold and plain, and the kingdom says your name when it says the craft. But the guild hall is shut to you. {npc} meets you outside its door, holding a stamp with your mark on it. "They will not let you stamp the bench," {he} says. "I had this made anyway. A master is a master."

choices.text: Ask {him} to help you earn the bench

effects.log: {npc} puts the stamp in your hand. "Teach two," {he} says. "Pay late. Then knock." You knock, a year later. The door opens.

choices.text: Stamp your own door with it

effects.log: Your mark goes on your own door, gold. The street knows it. The guild does not. It is enough, almost.

events.text: {npc} sits with you on the guild's bench after the masters have gone. "There is a thing the old masters did," {he} says. "Laid their tools down on this bench and became the mark. The one every master stamps on their work." {He} runs {his} thumb over the old mark. "Not yet. You have apprentices. But it is there."

choices.text: Say Dov and Ama come first

effects.log: "They do," says {npc}. "Good. That is why the bench would want you."

choices.text: Ask whose the old mark is

effects.log: "I have always thought it was the god's," says {npc}. "The first craftsman." You do not say anything at all.

events.text: {npc} turns your stamp over in {his} hands. "If you ever laid your tools down," {he} says, "lay them in my hands. Not on the bench. I would cut your name in the bench myself, so the guild could not forget you, whatever they think." {He} gives the stamp back. "That is a guild-mother's promise. They are worth something."

effects.log: {npc} shrugs. "You came back to the guild," {he} says. "Most do not. That is worth a name in wood."

choices.text: Say {he} is the best master in the kingdoms

effects.log: "I know," says {npc}. "Nobody stamps that, either."

events.text: The jade warms in your palm and writing rises on it, green as spring: [DEAR ANCESTOR. I AM LIO, OF YOUR HOUSE, FIVE HUNDRED YEARS FROM YOU. THE HOUSE NEEDS YOU.] In the house's old storeroom a young keeper of letters, {npc}, drops a box of scrolls. "That jade," {he} says. "The oldest letter in the house mentions it. I thought it was a story."

effects.log: {npc} reads it with {his} lips moving. "Five hundred years," {he} whispers. "Then the house lasts." {He} sits down on the box.

choices.text: Ask what the oldest letter says

effects.log: "That the god of {b10_world} gave the house its first hearth," says {npc}. "And that one day the house would write back to it." The jade, briefly, is hot.
