You write: I am here. The jade answers before you finish. [THANK YOU. HERE IS A GIFT.] There is money on the storeroom floor.

events.text: {npc}, keeper of your house's old letters, holds up a yellowed page. "Here," {he} says. "An ancestor wrote with the jade once. The descendants called that ancestor the one who held the house up from below." {He} looks at you, and at the jade warming in your hand. "The handwriting on this page is very like yours."

effects.log: {npc} lays the old page beside the jade, as if introducing them. The jade writes: [WELCOME BACK.] The storeroom smells, for a moment, of an old hearth.
It is a list of chores, mostly, and one line at the end: [THE KEEPER IS THE HOUSE'S HEART. TELL THEM.] You tell {him}.

events.text: Lio's second letter has missions, numbered like a farmer's list: [BRING A SPOUSE INTO THE HOUSE. RAISE A CHILD OF THE HOUSE. HOLD MONEY FOR THE HOUSE. MAKE THE HOUSE KNOWN IN THE KINGDOMS. LEAVE IT A CRAFT.] And under it: [EACH DONE, A GIFT FROM US.] {npc} reads over your shoulder. "Gifts," {he} says. "Or a house. Which are you doing it for?"

effects.log: You begin with the plainest: a craft, learned properly, for the house's hands. {npc} writes it in the letters. The jade glows warm and says nothing about gifts.
You ask Lio which mission pays best. The jade answers briskly: [MONEY. 2,000.] You start saving. {npc} rolls the letter up very carefully.

events.text: A letter comes through the jade, sad. [THE HOUSE IS POOR HERE. OUR ROOF LEAKS.] {npc} looks at your purse, then at you. "You could send something back," {he} says. "The oldest letters say it can be done. A coin buried under the hearth, for them to find. Or you could keep it, and ask what they will send."

effects.log: You bury them. A week later the jade writes: [WE FOUND IT! THE ROOF IS MENDED!] {npc} laughs aloud in the storeroom.
The jade is quiet for a day. Then: [WE WILL SEND WHAT WE CAN.] A small sum appears. You feel it is all they had.

events.text: The missions are slow because they are real. A spouse is not a mission; a child is not a mission; you live them, and the jade waits. {npc} keeps the letters in order. "The house five hundred years on is reading about this," {he} says. "Your wedding is in the letters. They are so happy about it."

choices.text: Write Lio about the ordinary days

effects.log: You write about bread and rain and the roof. Lio writes back: [THIS IS THE BEST LETTER IN THE HOUSE.] {npc} copies it twice.

choices.text: Ask {him} to read you the old letters

effects.log: {npc} reads them by the hearth. Your house, before you, was poor and loud and stubborn. You like it very much.

events.text: The gifts come, and the house grows rich on them. But Lio's letters grow shorter. [MISSION DONE. GIFT SENT.] Nothing else. {npc} lays the letters side by side on the storeroom floor. "Look," {he} says. "At first they wrote you whole pages. Now they write you receipts."

choices.text: Write Lio a whole page, no missions

effects.log: You write about the house: the roof, the keeper, the hearth. Lio's answer is long, and ends: [WE THOUGHT YOU ONLY WANTED GIFTS.] {npc} puts it at the top of the box.
The jade answers at once. A gift, a receipt. {npc} puts the letters back in the box and closes the lid.

events.text: A letter in a new hand comes through the jade, a child's: [I AM TAM, LIO'S DAUGHTER. I AM FIFTEEN. THEY SAY THE JADE TALKS TO A KIND VOICE AT FIFTEEN. IS THAT YOU?] {npc} goes very still. "The oldest letter says that too," {he} says. "A kind voice, at fifteen."

effects.log: You write to Tam about being fifteen, and what it was like, and that Tam is braver than Tam knows. Tam writes back a whole night.

choices.text: Send Tam a gift through the hearth

ok.log: Your coin turns up under Tam's hearth, five hundred years on, exactly where Tam was sitting. [IT WAS WARM!] Tam writes.

fail.log: The coin turns up in the wrong house, two streets away. Tam writes that the neighbours are very pleased.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to write to Tam too

effects.log: {npc} writes Tam three pages about the storeroom. Tam writes back: [I HAVE THE SAME BOX!] {npc} cries a little.

events.text: Ding. [THREE MISSIONS DONE.] The jade writes, in Lio's hand and Tam's together: [THE HOUSE STANDS. FIVE HUNDRED YEARS ON, BECAUSE OF YOU. WE READ YOUR LETTERS AT EVERY BIRTH.] {npc} sits in the storeroom with the box of letters in {his} lap, both ends of it: the first, and these. "The house is a letter," {he} says. "You just wrote the middle of it."

effects.log: You write the longest letter of your life. {npc} copies it into the house's box, to be found.
The first letter, from the god of {b10_world} giving the house its hearth, is in your hand. Of course it is.

events.text: Ding. [THREE MISSIONS DONE.] The jade writes: [THE HOUSE STANDS, FIVE HUNDRED YEARS ON. THANK YOU.] And then, after a long pause, in a child's hand: [TAM SAYS: DID YOU LOVE US? OR ONLY THE GIFTS?] {npc} does not look away. {He} waits, like the house waits.

effects.log: Tam writes back one line: [THAT IS ALL RIGHT. SO DID WE.] {npc} puts it in the box on top.
Tam writes back: [THEY DID.] It is true. It is not what Tam asked. {npc} files it away.

events.text: {npc} lays the jade on the box of letters. "Lio has written for the last time," {he} says. "The oldest letters say what comes after. The ancestor can answer with themself. Go forward into the jade. Be the kind voice a child of the house hears at fifteen." {He} touches the jade. "Not now. But Tam is reading. And so am I."

choices.text: Say you will be ready, one day

effects.log: "Not too soon," says {npc}. "The house here still needs you."
You write Tam a goodnight across five hundred years. The jade is warm all night.

events.text: {npc} holds out {his} hands for the last letter. "If you go forward," {he} says, "send the last one in my hands. I will read it at every wedding of the house until I am old, and then I will teach the next keeper to." {He} smiles, a little crookedly. "I would like the house to hear you. Not only the gifts."

effects.log: {npc} nods and puts a blank page in the box, waiting for it.
"The old letters say that about every keeper," says {npc}. "Well. They are right."
